questions.q: A 28-year-old man from rural India presents with a hypopigmented patch on his forearm with loss of sensation to light touch and temperature. Slit-skin smear shows no AFB. Nerve biopsy reveals lymphocytic infiltration with well-formed granulomas but no AFB. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Tuberculoid leprosy (TT) presents with a single or few well-defined hypopigmented anesthetic patches. Histology shows well-formed epithelioid granulomas with lymphocytes; AFB are absent. It is paucibacillary with high cell-mediated immunity.

questions.q: A 35-year-old HIV-positive patient (CD4 count 50 cells/µL) presents with verrucous, crusted plaques on the hands and feet. Microscopy of skin scrapings shows numerous mites at all stages. What is the recommended treatment?
opts: Oral ivermectin 200 µg/kg single dose only
Oral ivermectin 200 µg/kg combined with topical keratolytics, repeat doses weekly
questions.exp: Crusted (Norwegian) scabies in immunocompromised patients requires combination therapy with oral ivermectin (repeated doses) plus keratolytics (e.g., 5% salicylic acid) to reduce the thick crust and allow drug penetration. Single-dose monotherapy is insufficient in this setting.

questions.q: A 22-year-old presents with a painless, indurated genital ulcer with a clean base. Dark-field microscopy reveals mobile spiral organisms with regular tight coils. Which organism is responsible?
questions.exp: A painless, indurated, clean-based genital ulcer (chancre) with Treponema pallidum on dark-field microscopy is the classic presentation of primary syphilis. H. ducreyi causes painful, soft, dirty-based ulcers. C. granulomatis causes donovanosis with beefy-red ulcers.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with tense bullae on normal-appearing skin and mucous membrane sparing. ELISA shows antibodies against BP180 and BP230. What is the target structure?
opts: Hemidesmosome components at the dermal-epidermal junction
Type VII collagen in anchoring fibrils
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) targets BP180 (type XVII collagen) and BP230, both components of hemidesmosomes at the basement membrane zone. This leads to subepidermal blistering with tense bullae on normal or erythematous skin, typically sparing mucous membranes.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man presents with flaccid bullae that rupture easily leaving erosions on the scalp, face, and oral mucosa. Nikolsky's sign is positive. Direct immunofluorescence shows IgG deposition in a 'fishnet' pattern throughout the epidermis. What is the target antigen?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris with mucocutaneous involvement carries antibodies against both Desmoglein 1 and Desmoglein 3. Mucosal-only PV targets Dsg3 alone. Paraneoplastic pemphigus targets envoplakin and periplakin (and other plakin family proteins).

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with painful oral erosions, erythema multiforme-like lesions, and conjunctival injection following trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole therapy. She has >10% body surface area epidermal detachment. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Immediate transfer to a burns ICU and withdrawal of the offending drug
questions.exp: This is SJS/TEN overlap (10-30% BSA). The cornerstone of management is immediate withdrawal of the causative drug and transfer to a burns unit for fluid/electrolyte management, wound care, and nutritional support. Steroids are controversial. Supportive care in a burns unit is the immediate priority.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man presents with pruritic, violaceous, flat-topped polygonal papules on the flexural aspect of wrists. Wickham's striae are visible. Biopsy shows a saw-tooth pattern of the rete ridges with a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the DEJ and colloid bodies. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Lichen planus classically presents with the 4 Ps: Pruritic, Purple (violaceous), Polygonal, Papules. Wickham's striae are pathognomonic. Histology shows saw-toothed rete ridges, band-like lymphocytic infiltrate hugging the DEJ, and colloid (Civatte) bodies representing dyskeratotic keratinocytes.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with erythematous plaques with silvery scales on the elbows and scalp, nail pitting, and onycholysis. Auspitz sign is positive. The Koebner phenomenon is present. What is the characteristic histological finding?
opts: Acanthosis with parakeratosis, Munro microabscesses, and spongiform pustules of Kogoj
Perifollicular lymphocytic infiltrate with hair follicle destruction
Band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the DEJ with colloid bodies
questions.exp: Psoriasis histology shows regular acanthosis (elongated and clubbed rete ridges), parakeratosis (nuclei in stratum corneum), Munro microabscesses (neutrophils in SC), and spongiform pustules of Kogoj in the spinous layer. Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding on scale removal) is due to thin suprapapillary plates.

questions.q: A 32-year-old man presents with a well-defined annular plaque with central clearing and an active scaly border on his thigh. KOH preparation shows septate hyphae with arthroconidia. He plays contact sports. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.exp: Tinea corporis (ringworm) in adults, especially athletes (tinea gladiatorum), is most commonly caused by Trichophyton rubrum. It presents as an annular erythematous plaque with a scaly advancing border and central clearing.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with thick, greenish-yellow nail discoloration of all fingernails associated with chronic respiratory tract infections. Culture under the onycholytic nail plate grows Pseudomonas aeruginosa. What sign/condition is classically described?
questions.exp: Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonizes the subungual space under onycholytic nails, producing pyocyanin pigment causing green-black discoloration — green nail syndrome (chloronychia). Treatment involves trimming the onycholytic portion and topical antibiotics (polymyxin B, nalidixic acid).

questions.q: A 60-year-old diabetic man presents with a rapidly expanding painful plaque on the leg with violaceous borders, blistering, and grey skin discoloration. The wound appears deeper than expected. Which organism is the most common cause of Type II (monomicrobial) necrotizing fasciitis?
questions.exp: Necrotizing fasciitis type II (monomicrobial) is most commonly caused by Group A Streptococcus. It presents with rapidly spreading necrosis, severe pain out of proportion to appearance, and systemic sepsis. Diabetes, obesity, and immunosuppression are risk factors. Clostridium causes gas gangrene. Type I is polymicrobial.

questions.q: A 35-year-old immunocompetent patient presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base along the T4 dermatome on the left chest, with severe lancinating pain preceding the eruption by 3 days. What is the treatment of choice?
opts: Oral acyclovir 800 mg 5 times daily for 7 days
Oral valacyclovir 1000 mg three times daily for 7 days
questions.exp: Herpes zoster in an immunocompetent adult is best treated with oral valacyclovir 1000 mg TID for 7 days (or famciclovir 500 mg TID). Valacyclovir achieves better bioavailability than acyclovir. IV acyclovir is reserved for disseminated, ophthalmic, or immunocompromised cases.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with a painless papule on her lower lip that slowly grew into a firm, skin-colored nodule over 2 months. Biopsy shows a cyst lined by stratified squamous epithelium filled with laminated keratin, WITH a prominent granular cell layer. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Epidermoid (infundibular) cysts are lined by stratified squamous epithelium WITH a prominent granular layer and are filled with laminated keratin. Trichilemmal (pilar) cysts lack a granular layer and are filled with homogeneous eosinophilic keratin; they occur predominantly on the scalp.

questions.q: A 70-year-old fair-skinned farmer presents with a pearly, translucent papule with rolled edges and telangiectasia on his nose. Biopsy shows islands of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and stromal retraction artefact. What is the most common anatomical site for this tumour?
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common skin malignancy and most commonly arises on the nose (followed by periocular region, cheek, and forehead). The classic nodular BCC shows basaloid cell islands with peripheral nuclear palisading and peritumoral stromal retraction (clefting artefact).

questions.q: A 65-year-old woman presents with a rapidly growing, firm nodule with a central keratin-filled crater on her forearm appearing over 6 weeks, now 2 cm. Histology shows a cup-shaped crater with well-differentiated squamous epithelium and glassy cytoplasm. What is the best management?
opts: Watchful waiting for 3 months as lesion may self-resolve
questions.exp: Keratoacanthoma (KA) is a rapidly growing squamoproliferative tumour that may represent a well-differentiated SCC variant. Despite its potential for self-resolution, surgical excision is preferred to provide histological certainty, since SCC cannot be excluded clinically.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with a butterfly-shaped erythematous rash on the malar region, photosensitivity, and oral ulcers. Anti-dsDNA antibodies are elevated. ANA is positive at 1:640. What is the most SPECIFIC antibody for this condition?
questions.exp: Anti-Sm (anti-Smith) antibody is the most SPECIFIC antibody for SLE (~99% specific), though found in only 25-30% of patients (less sensitive). Anti-dsDNA is highly specific (~70%) and correlates with disease activity. ANA is the most sensitive (~99%) but least specific screening test.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman presents with tightening of skin on her fingers (sclerodactyly), Raynaud's phenomenon, calcinosis, and telangiectasias on the face. She is diagnosed with CREST syndrome. Which autoantibody is most strongly associated with CREST/limited cutaneous SSc?
questions.exp: Anti-centromere antibody (ACA) is strongly associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc/CREST syndrome). Anti-Scl-70 is associated with diffuse cutaneous SSc and pulmonary fibrosis. Anti-RNA pol III correlates with diffuse SSc and renal crisis.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with proximal muscle weakness, heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules over knuckles, and raised CK levels. What is the skin finding that is PATHOGNOMONIC for this diagnosis?
questions.exp: Gottron's papules — violaceous, flat-topped papules over the dorsal MCP and IP joints — are PATHOGNOMONIC for dermatomyositis. Heliotrope rash and V-sign are highly characteristic but not pathognomonic. Mechanic's hands occur in antisynthetase syndrome.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with honey-colored crusted lesions around the nose and mouth. Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters. The child has widespread lesions involving the trunk. Which treatment is most appropriate?
questions.exp: Non-bullous impetigo (caused by S. aureus and/or S. pyogenes) with widespread lesions requires systemic antibiotics; cefalexin (a first-generation cephalosporin) is preferred. Topical mupirocin/retapamulin is adequate for localized disease. Amoxicillin alone misses penicillinase-producing S. aureus.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man who returned from a tropical region presents with a painless, progressive genital ulcer with a 'beef-red' granulomatous base and satellite lesions. Biopsy shows Donovan bodies inside mononuclear cells. What stain best demonstrates these inclusions?
questions.exp: Donovanosis (granuloma inguinale) is caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. Donovan bodies — dark-staining intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies in mononuclear cells — are best demonstrated by Giemsa stain (or Leishman, Wright stain). ZN stain is for mycobacteria, PAS for fungi, and Warthin-Starry for Treponema and Bartonella.

questions.q: A 20-year-old man presents with multiple, firm, flesh-colored nodules with central umbilication on the penile shaft and perianal region. They have appeared over 3 months and he reports multiple sexual partners. What is the pathognomonic histological feature?
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by a poxvirus. The pathognomonic histological finding is large eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies called Henderson-Paterson bodies (molluscum bodies), which compress the nucleus peripherally. Koilocytes are seen with HPV infection.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with palpable purpura on the lower extremities, arthralgias, and microscopic haematuria. Biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA deposits on direct immunofluorescence. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein Purpura) is characterized by palpable purpura, arthritis/arthralgia, renal involvement, and abdominal pain. DIF shows IgA deposits in vessel walls, differentiating it from other forms of leukocytoclastic vasculitis.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man on long-term hydroxychloroquine for RA presents with blue-gray pigmentation on the shins and nails. His visual field examination reveals a bull's-eye maculopathy. Which monitoring guideline should be followed to prevent this complication?
opts: Baseline and annual ophthalmologic screening after 5 years of use
questions.exp: Hydroxychloroquine can cause irreversible retinal toxicity (bull's-eye maculopathy) with prolonged use or high doses. Baseline ophthalmologic examination and annual screening after 5 years (or earlier if high-risk) is mandatory to detect early toxicity. It also causes blue-gray cutaneous pigmentation.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with recurrent oral aphthous ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis. His pathergy test is positive (2 mm papule at sterile needle-prick site at 48 hours). What is the diagnostic significance of the pathergy test in this condition?
opts: Hyperreactivity to minor trauma — a defining feature in Middle Eastern and Asian patients with this diagnosis
Elevated ESR and CRP after needle puncture
Formation of subepidermal blisters at the site of trauma
Psoriatic plaque formation at sites of injury
questions.exp: Behçet's disease pathergy test: a 2 mm papule or pustule at a sterile intradermal needle-prick site at 24-48 hours indicates cutaneous hyperreactivity to minor trauma. The International Study Group criteria for Behçet's include recurrent oral ulcers plus 2 of: genital ulcers, eye lesions, skin lesions, or positive pathergy.

questions.q: A 10-year-old child with patchy hair loss and scalp scaling shows bright green fluorescence under Wood's lamp examination. Culture on Sabouraud's medium shows a flat, powdery colony with yellowish reverse. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Microsporum canis causes ectothrix tinea capitis and produces bright green fluorescence under Wood's lamp (due to pteridine metabolites). Trichophyton tonsurans and T. violaceum cause endothrix infections and do NOT fluoresce. T. schoenleinii (favus) shows pale green/grey fluorescence.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes presents with black necrotic eschar within the nasal cavity extending to the palate, facial pain, and proptosis. Biopsy shows broad non-septate hyphae branching at right angles with vascular invasion. What is the treatment of choice?
opts: Surgical debridement plus IV liposomal amphotericin B
questions.exp: Rhinocerebral mucormycosis (caused by Mucor/Rhizopus spp.) presents with black eschar and rapid orbital/cerebral spread in diabetic ketoacidosis. Histology shows broad (10-20 µm), non-septate hyphae at right angles. Treatment requires aggressive surgical debridement plus IV liposomal amphotericin B. Voriconazole and fluconazole have no activity against Mucorales.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with excessive hair loss from the crown and frontoparietal region with preserved frontal hairline. She uses an androgenic progestogen-containing OCP. Trichoscopy shows follicular miniaturization and >20% shaft diameter variation. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Topical minoxidil 5% and switch to a low-androgenic OCP immediately
Topical minoxidil 2% plus finasteride 1 mg daily
Assess serum ferritin, thyroid function, androgens, and DHEAS before initiating treatment
questions.exp: Female pattern hair loss (FPHL) requires evaluation of treatable underlying causes first: serum ferritin (iron deficiency), thyroid function, androgens (testosterone, DHEAS) to exclude hyperandrogenism. The current androgenic OCP may be contributing. Treating reversible causes before starting specific therapy is the priority.

questions.q: A 5-year-old child presents with diffuse erythroderma, generalized superficial erosions, perioral crusting, and positive Nikolsky's sign. There is no mucosal involvement. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus phage group II. What is the mechanism of tissue injury?
opts: Direct bacterial invasion of the epidermis
Type III hypersensitivity immune complex deposition
Exfoliative toxin (ET-A and ET-B) cleaving desmoglein 1 in the granular layer
questions.exp: Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS) is caused by exfoliative toxins A and B produced by S. aureus phage group II. These toxins are serine proteases that specifically cleave desmoglein 1 in the granular layer, causing superficial intraepidermal splitting. This distinguishes SSSS from TEN (subepidermal, T-cell mediated).

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman with long-standing lepromatous leprosy on multidrug therapy suddenly develops fever, painful erythematous nodules on the arms and thighs, tender lymphadenopathy, and iritis. Biopsy of a nodule shows neutrophilic infiltrate with necrosis. What is this reaction and its treatment?
opts: Type 2 reaction (ENL) — treated with thalidomide or prednisolone
Downgrading reaction — no additional treatment needed
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL) is a Type 2 lepra reaction occurring in BL/LL leprosy. It is immune complex-mediated (Type III hypersensitivity). Features include tender erythematous nodules, fever, iritis, and orchitis. Treatment is thalidomide (drug of choice, males) or corticosteroids (females, contraindicated cases). Type 1 reactions are treated with prednisolone.

questions.q: A 48-year-old man with chronic arsenic exposure presents with palmoplantar keratoses and a wart-like growth on his hand dorsum. Biopsy shows atypical squamous cells with full-thickness epidermal dysplasia and no dermal invasion. What is this condition?
opts: Arsenical keratosis progressing to invasive SCC
Bowen's disease (squamous cell carcinoma in situ)
questions.exp: Bowen's disease is SCC in situ characterized by full-thickness epidermal dysplasia with intact basement membrane. Risk factors include arsenic exposure, HPV (types 16, 18), UV radiation, and immunosuppression. Erythroplasia of Queyrat is Bowen's disease on the glans penis. Actinic keratosis shows only partial-thickness (lower zone) dysplasia.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis is started on methotrexate. Before initiating therapy, which baseline investigation is most critical to assess hepatotoxicity risk?
opts: Procollagen III N-terminal peptide (PIIINP) serum level
Clinical risk assessment with LFTs, hepatitis serology, and FibroScan if indicated
questions.exp: Before starting methotrexate for psoriasis, hepatotoxicity risk is assessed with LFTs, serum albumin, and hepatitis B/C serology. Current guidelines (BAD, AAD) recommend non-invasive liver fibrosis assessment (FibroScan/transient elastography) and clinical risk factor assessment in place of routine pre-treatment liver biopsy. PIIINP is used for monitoring during treatment in some guidelines.
